profile.reading: Crane Data Centers is a data center operator whose own site emphasizes sustainability and advanced infrastructure. Its Oregon facility sits in Forest Grove, Oregon, about 8 miles from Hillsboro airport, and is described across two named developments, PDX01, delivered in two 24 megawatt phases, and PDX02 at approximately 48 megawatts, for a combined capacity exceeding 100 megawatts once complete. The companys site states the facility will be ready for service in the third quarter of 2026, with high-density cooling supporting more than 667 watts per square foot, multiple fiber paths, sustainable technologies, and redundant power transmission feeds with access to renewable energy sources. The pages fetched during this research session did not include company headquarters, founding history, or other data center locations beyond this Oregon campus, so Crane Data Centers broader corporate profile remains not published as of the research date.

reading.body:
Crane DC - Portland publishes 36,000 square feet of technical space but no megawatt figure, making its capacity for AI workloads unknowable without power specifications.

The seven certifications on record qualify the campus for specific workload categories. PCI DSS qualifies it for payment card data. FISMA and NIST 800-53 together qualify it for federal information systems. HITRUST qualifies it for healthcare information. ISO 27001 and SSAE 18 qualify it for enterprise tenants requiring audited information security management and controls reporting. LEED indicates the building met a green construction or operations standard at the time of certification.

For an AI decision, the missing power number is the central fact. Compute density for training workloads is the binding constraint, and 36,000 square feet of technical space could support very different capacities depending on power delivery, cooling infrastructure, and floor loading, none of which are published. The compliance portfolio suggests the operator targets regulated enterprise and government workloads rather than hyperscale AI training, but that inference rests on the certification mix alone, not on any published tenant or use-case claim.

This facility represents a broader pattern in Oregon, where only six of 133 mapped data centers have published any megawatt capacity at all, and those six total 182 MW. The absence of disclosed power specifications makes it impossible to assess the state's aggregate contribution to AI infrastructure.
